document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: EANO updated its evidence-based guidance because diagnostic approaches changed substantially and mature results became available from major clinical trials. The guidance addresses diagnosis, treatment and follow-up for adults with diffuse gliomas. Its diagnostic framework uses the 2016 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System and subsequent cIMPACT-NOW recommendations. Treatment guidance draws on practice-changing trials and addresses neuropathological and neuroradiological assessment, surgery, radiotherapy and systemic pharmacotherapy. The intended readers include professionals caring for adults with diffuse gliomas, patients, caregivers and health-care providers.

document_sections.heading: EANO guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of diffuse gliomas of adulthood
document_sections.content: The 2016 revision of the WHO classification and later cIMPACT-NOW proposals substantially changed glioma taxonomy. Molecular findings can now establish a glioblastoma diagnosis alongside histology, and the term ‘IDH-mutant glioblastoma’ is being discontinued. This guidance addresses prevention, early diagnosis, screening, integrated histomolecular diagnosis, treatment and follow-up in adults with diffuse gliomas. Differential diagnosis, treatment adverse effects, and supportive and palliative care are outside its stated scope.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: An EANO Executive Board-appointed, multinational task force representing disciplines involved in adult glioma care prepared the guidance. PubMed searches covered January 2011 to July 2020 and used ‘glioma’, ‘anaplastic’, ‘astrocytoma’, ‘oligodendroglioma’, ‘glioblastoma’, ‘trial’, ‘clinical’, ‘surgery’, ‘radiotherapy’ and ‘chemotherapy’; the authors also searched their own libraries. The review considered English-language publications, with abstract-only information accepted exceptionally. References were selected for relevance to the guidance's broad scope. Consensus arose through repeated manuscript circulation and telephone discussions of disputed topics. Key recommendations carry a class of evidence, C, and level of recommendation, L.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology and prevention
document_sections.content: Worldwide annual glioma incidence is approximately six cases per 100,000 individuals. Men have a 1.6-fold greater likelihood of diagnosis than women. The vast majority of gliomas are sporadic, although neurofibromatosis type I, tuberous sclerosis, Turcot syndrome, Li–Fraumeni syndrome and Lynch syndrome are associated with gliomagenesis. For people with these syndromes, neuroimaging screening is confined to the initial diagnostic work-up; further imaging is not indicated unless new findings such as seizures, aphasia, hemiparesis or sensory deficits suggest an intracranial lesion. Counselling and screening asymptomatic relatives who carry gliomagenesis-associated germline mutations requires caution and collaboration with clinical geneticists. No measure is known to prevent glioma development.

document_sections.heading: History and clinical examination
document_sections.content: The duration of neurological manifestations helps estimate growth rate: symptoms arising only weeks before diagnosis generally suggest faster growth, whereas symptoms present for years generally suggest slower growth. During the year before diagnosis, most reported manifestations are nonspecific, including fatigue and headache. History-taking can reveal familial susceptibility or uncommon external risks, such as radiation exposure; relatives may be needed to obtain a reliable account. Firm guidance remains to be developed on involving family members and caregivers and assessing decision-making capacity. Presentations include new epilepsy, focal motor or sensory deficits, cognitive impairment and features of raised intracranial pressure. Examination seeks evidence of systemic cancer, to distinguish a primary brain tumour from metastasis, and contraindications to neurosurgery. NANO can document aspects of neurological function. Standardized neurocognitive batteries are increasingly used in addition to performance-status assessment, MMSE or MoCA. Despite limitations, MMSE remains widely used for cognitive screening and is freely available for individual use.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations.
document_sections.content: Clinical decisions should account for KPS, neurological function, age, and patient-specific risks and benefits (C: IV; L: A). Screening and prevention have no substantial role for patients with gliomas (C: IV; L: C). Patients with relevant germline variants or suspected inherited cancer syndromes should receive genetic counselling and might then undergo molecular genetic testing (C: IV; L: C).

document_sections.heading: Box 1 | Key new developments in the diagnosis and management of gliomas (2016–2020)
document_sections.content: Glioblastoma is characterized as a diffuse astrocytic glioma without IDH or histone H3 mutations and with microvascular proliferation, necrosis and/or TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification or a +7/–10 signature. The former designation IDH-mutant glioblastoma is replaced by IDH-mutant astrocytoma, WHO grade 4; homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion also identifies WHO grade 4 in IDH-mutant astrocytoma. H3.3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma is a newly recognized WHO grade 4 entity. The usefulness of distinguishing WHO grades 2 and 3 within IDH-mutant gliomas is increasingly questioned, and CODEL and EORTC 1635 enrol both grades. In CATNON, radiotherapy with maintenance temozolomide extended survival only for IDH-mutant WHO grade 3 gliomas, not tumours diagnosed as IDH-wild-type anaplastic gliomas. Increasing maintenance temozolomide from 6 to 12 cycles extends neither PFS nor OS. Bevacizumab extends neither PFS nor OS in recurrent WHO grade 2 or 3 glioma without 1p/19q codeletion. For recurrent glioblastoma, nivolumab is not superior to bevacizumab; for newly diagnosed glioblastoma without MGMT promoter methylation, it is not superior to temozolomide.

document_sections.heading: Preoperative diagnostics
document_sections.content: The diagnostic imaging standard for a suspected brain tumour is MRI with T2-weighted, FLAIR and 3D T1-weighted sequences acquired before and after gadolinium-based contrast. Perfusion MRI and amino acid PET can identify metabolic hotspots to guide sampling, particularly when biopsy rather than open resection is planned. Electroencephalography can assist with monitoring tumour-related epilepsy or investigating altered consciousness. Studies have detected cell-free tumour DNA in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, but clinical benefit from liquid biopsy for screening, early detection or preoperative assessment remains unproven.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations.
document_sections.content: MRI before and after gadolinium-based contrast is the preferred initial diagnostic imaging method (C: IV; L: B). When imaging abnormalities increase during the first months after a local intervention, including radiotherapy or an experimental local treatment, pseudoprogression should be considered (C: IV; L: B).

document_sections.heading: Preoperative management
document_sections.content: Preoperative care should follow written local procedures and multidisciplinary discussion, ideally in a dedicated tumour board with neuroradiology, neuropathology, neurosurgery, radiation oncology and specialist neuro-oncology participation, plus paediatric oncology when needed. Corticosteroids can reduce symptomatic tumour-associated oedema before surgery unless primary cerebral lymphoma or an inflammatory lesion is suspected. Osmotic agents and other pharmacological alternatives are seldom needed. Patients who have experienced seizures should receive anticonvulsants before surgery. Primary anticonvulsant prophylaxis does not lower first-seizure risk in patients with glioma who have never had a seizure.

document_sections.heading: Tissue acquisition
document_sections.content: Treatment selection depends on a tissue diagnosis that includes relevant molecular markers, so initial surgery commonly serves both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Specialist neurosurgeons in high-volume centres should manage glioma surgery. Palliative management without histological confirmation should generally be avoided, except when biopsy risk is too high or prognosis is likely very unfavourable, such as with substantial comorbidity, a large radiologically typical glioblastoma and rapid neurological decline. A definitive diagnosis helps counsel patients and caregivers even if no additional tumour-directed treatment is advised. When safe microsurgical resection is impracticable because of location or clinical condition, stereotactic biopsy should be performed. Frame-based and frame-less approaches have low morbidity and high diagnostic accuracy. Serial specimens along the needle trajectory reduce sampling bias; experienced teams can obtain material adequate for molecular profiling. IDH mutations, 1p/19q codeletion and MGMT promoter methylation are relatively homogeneous within tumours, making sampling error for these markers unlikely. For other markers without demonstrated homogeneity, stereotactic or open sampling should include different tumour regions. Intraoperative 5-aminolevulinic acid fluorescence can help confirm adequate stereotactic sampling. Some centres favour open biopsy to secure enough material for possible molecular studies.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations.
document_sections.content: Making clinical decisions without a tissue diagnosis should be contemplated only under very exceptional circumstances (C: IV; L: not applicable).

document_sections.heading: Fig. 1 | Diagnostic algorithm for the integrated classification of the major diffuse gliomas in adults.
document_sections.content: The algorithm links histology, site and molecular findings to integrated diagnoses of oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, H3.3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma and H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma. Biopsy specimens are routinely assessed by immunohistochemistry for IDH1 R132H and nuclear ATRX loss. For a histologically typical glioblastoma in a patient aged >55 years, with no preceding lower-grade glioma, a non-midline location and retained nuclear ATRX, negative IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry is sufficient to classify IDH-wild-type glioblastoma. Other diffuse gliomas negative for IDH1 R132H require IDH1 and IDH2 sequencing for non-canonical mutations. IDH-wild-type diffuse astrocytic gliomas without necrosis or microvascular proliferation require assessment of EGFR amplification, TERT promoter mutation and +7/–10. H3.3 G34R/V testing by immunohistochemistry or sequencing is particularly relevant to young patients with IDH-wild-type gliomas, including those <50 years of age with tumour-cell nuclear ATRX loss. Diffuse tumours of the thalamus, brainstem or spinal cord require assessment of H3 K27M and nuclear H3K27me3 loss.

document_sections.heading: Integrated histomolecular classification
document_sections.content: Intraoperative cytology or frozen-section assessment checks whether enough tumour has been collected. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue supports histology, immunohistochemistry, molecular genetics and cytogenetics; tissue should also be cryopreserved when feasible for assays requiring high-quality DNA or RNA. Classification integrates histological type, grade and molecular findings under the 2016 WHO framework and cIMPACT-NOW updates. ‘Not otherwise specified’ applies when subtype-defining markers were not tested or results were inconclusive. Principal adult diffuse-glioma biomarkers include IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion, histone H3 K27M, histone H3.3 G34R/V, TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, +7/–10 and homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion at 9p21. IDH1 codon 132 or IDH2 codon 172 missense mutations define IDH-mutant astrocytomas and are associated with G-CIMP. Histological WHO grade 2 or 3 diffuse gliomas negative for IDH1 R132H by immunohistochemistry require sequencing for uncommon IDH1 and IDH2 mutations. IDH-mutant astrocytomas usually show nuclear ATRX loss and TP53 mutation and, by definition, lack 1p/19q codeletion. Nuclear ATRX loss in an IDH-mutant glioma establishes astrocytic lineage without separate 1p/19q testing; retained ATRX calls for 1p/19q analysis. Separate ATRX immunohistochemistry is unnecessary if a broader assay establishes both IDH and 1p/19q status. IDH-mutant astrocytomas are assigned WHO grade 2, 3 or 4. The former term ‘glioblastoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4’ is replaced by ‘astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4’, because these tumours differ biologically from IDH-wild-type glioblastoma despite similar histology. Necrosis, microvascular proliferation and homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion can identify grade 4; the deletion also indicates poor prognosis. Arabic rather than roman grade numerals are used because II and III can be confused.

document_sections.heading: Table 1 | Molecular markers for the diagnosis and management of gliomas
document_sections.content: The table sets out molecular markers, the biological functions of affected genes and their diagnostic or management roles. It covers IDH1 R132 or IDH2 R172 mutation, 1p/19q codeletion, nuclear ATRX loss, histone H3 K27M, histone H3.3 G34R/V, MGMT promoter methylation, homozygous CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion, EGFR amplification, TERT promoter mutation, +7/–10 and BRAFV600E. MGMT promoter methylation is predictive of benefit from alkylating chemotherapy in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma rather than a diagnostic marker. The table also identifies CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion as associated with poor outcome and WHO grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma, and describes BRAFV600E as rare in adult diffuse gliomas but potentially amenable to pharmacological intervention.

document_sections.heading: Integrated histomolecular classification
document_sections.content: Brainstem or cerebellar diffuse astrocytomas warrant particular attention: non-canonical IDH mutations occur in ~80% of infratentorial astrocytomas versus <10% of supratentorial astrocytomas. Reliance on IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry alone can therefore misclassify infratentorial disease; sequencing for uncommon IDH1 and IDH2 variants is required. Only ~50% of infratentorial IDH-mutant astrocytomas exhibit nuclear ATRX loss or MGMT promoter methylation. Oligodendroglial tumours require both IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion. Histological anaplasia distinguishes WHO grade 3 from grade 2; molecular grading criteria are undefined, although CDKN2A homozygous deletion at 9p21 has been associated with shorter survival. Oligoastrocytoma is no longer considered a distinct subtype because it lacks a characteristic genetic profile. Diffuse astrocytic tumours with wild-type IDH and histone H3 and either necrosis or microvascular proliferation are WHO grade 4 IDH-wild-type glioblastomas. Without these histological features, EGFR amplification, TERT promoter mutation or +7/–10 also supports that classification because of its association with poor prognosis. Tumours lacking all these findings and not assignable elsewhere are rare, occur more often in children, adolescents or young adults, and require further molecular investigation. H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, WHO grade 4 is a diffuse midline tumour with a histone H3.3 or H3.1 amino-acid 27 lysine-to-methionine substitution; nuclear H3 K27M staining with loss of H3K27me3 is characteristic. H3.3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma, WHO grade 4 is a proposed malignant subtype with H3F3A codon 34 missense mutation.

document_sections.heading: Integrated histomolecular classification
document_sections.content: MGMT promoter methylation has limited diagnostic utility but helps predict benefit from alkylating agents in glioblastoma and other IDH-wild-type gliomas. Methylation-specific PCR, pyrosequencing or methylation arrays such as MGMT-STP27 can determine status; immunocytochemistry cannot do so adequately. Remaining challenges are interlaboratory agreement and the outcome implications of limited methylation between methylated and unmethylated states. Next-generation sequencing panels might capture most diagnostically relevant genetic and chromosomal changes in one assay. Array-based DNA methylation profiling offers a useful histology-independent diagnostic method. RNA sequencing may detect diagnostically or predictively relevant oncogenic fusions in rare diffuse gliomas, chiefly IDH-wild-type glioblastomas. Molecular workflows should be standardized without delaying radiotherapy or tumour-specific medication.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations.
document_sections.content: Gliomas should be classified using the most recent WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System together with cIMPACT-NOW updates (C: IV; L: B). Routine diffuse-glioma diagnosis should include immunohistochemistry for IDH1 R132H and nuclear ATRX (C: IV; L: B). If IDH1 R132H staining is negative, IDH1 codon 132 and IDH2 codon 172 should be sequenced in every WHO grade 2 or 3 diffuse astrocytic or oligodendroglial glioma and every glioblastoma in a patient aged <55 years (C: IV; L: B). All IDH-mutant gliomas retaining nuclear ATRX expression should undergo 1p/19q codeletion testing (C: II; L: B). MGMT promoter methylation should be assessed in glioblastoma, especially for older or frail patients, to inform temozolomide use (C: I; L: B). Homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion should be investigated in IDH-mutant astrocytomas (C: IV; L: B). IDH-wild-type diffuse gliomas lacking grade 4-defining necrosis and microvascular proliferation should be tested for +7/–10, EGFR amplification and TERT promoter mutation to permit diagnosis of IDH-wild-type glioblastoma (C: IV; L: B). Diffuse midline gliomas should undergo H3 K27M assessment (C: IV; L: B). BRAFV600 testing might be considered in IDH-wild-type diffuse gliomas (C: IV; L: C).

document_sections.heading: Therapy — general recommendations
document_sections.content: General management addresses prognostic factors, surgery, radiotherapy, systemic treatment, disease monitoring and patient support.

document_sections.heading: Prognostic factors.
document_sections.content: Younger age and better performance status at diagnosis predict more favourable outcomes independently of treatment. Although IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion previously had major prognostic value, since 2016 they have defined disease entities and consequently are not prognostic within an individual subtype. With alkylating chemotherapy used in the vast majority of adults with glioma, MGMT promoter methylation is described as the most important remaining prognostic factor.

document_sections.heading: Surgical therapy.
document_sections.content: Surgery aims to remove the greatest safely achievable tumour volume while preserving neurological function. Navigation incorporating functional MRI or diffusion tensor imaging, intraoperative MRI or ultrasound, functional monitoring and 5-aminolevulinic acid fluorescence can reduce residual tumour without increasing new deficits. Evoked potentials, electromyography and awake mapping can help protect language and cognition in eloquent regions. Avoiding permanent deficits takes precedence over resection extent because surgery does not cure diffuse glioma; deficits can compromise independence, QOL and subsequent treatment. A predicted minor deficit, such as quadrantanopia, may exceptionally be accepted after thorough shared decision-making, while unpredictable surgical risks must also be explained. Postoperative complications and deficits adversely affect prognosis and further care. Within 24–48 hours, resection extent should be assessed by MRI, or CT if MRI is unavailable, before and after contrast; MRI should include diffusion-weighted imaging for perioperative ischaemia. The prognostic interpretation of resection extent and residual volume remains disputed because relevant RCTs are exceptionally difficult and nearly absent. Lower resection extent and larger residual volumes are associated with worse prognosis across grades and subtypes, but causation remains uncertain. Absolute enhancing and non-enhancing residual volume may matter more than percentage removed. Starting postoperative radiotherapy early (<3 weeks) rather than later (3–5 weeks) has not correlated with better OS. Resectability may reflect less malignant biology: prospective findings showed more gross-total resections in IDH-mutant than IDH-wild-type tumours, and retrospective findings showed biopsy was more often the first operation in IDH-wild-type disease. Longer survival in IDH-mutant disease should therefore not simply be credited to gross-total resection. These limitations of retrospective uncontrolled evidence do not negate efforts toward safe complete removal.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations.
document_sections.content: Because resection extent is prognostic, attempting complete removal is justified for all glioma entities (C: IV; L: B). Prevention of a new permanent neurological deficit has greater priority than resection extent in contemporary glioma surgery (C: IV; L: C).

document_sections.heading: Radiotherapy.
document_sections.content: Radiotherapy seeks better local control without neurotoxicity; earlier trials found delayed neurological deterioration and longer survival. Subtype, age, KPS and residual volume guide its timing and schedule. Treatment should begin within 3–5 weeks after surgery and commonly delivers 50–60 Gy in 1.8–2 Gy daily fractions. Evidence does not suggest an added benefit from higher versus lower doses in WHO grade 2 glioma; randomized studies do not support >60 Gy for higher grades. Hypofractionation, for example 15 × 2.67 Gy, is appropriate for older patients (>65–70 years of age) and those with poor prognosis, typically KPS <70. Gross tumour volume comprises the operative bed and residual tumour visible on T1-weighted, T2-weighted and FLAIR MRI. A 1.0–2.0 cm margin accounts for microscopic invasion when defining clinical target volume, with adjustment for T2-weighted or FLAIR abnormalities and anatomical boundaries. A further margin, usually 0.3–0.5 cm, covers positioning and delivery uncertainties. Amino acid PET-guided delineation has been studied but is not routine practice. Radiation-sensitive structures should be outlined, including optic pathways, retinae, lenses, brainstem, pituitary, cochleae and hippocampi. Conformal techniques may improve coverage and spare unaffected brain; intensity-modulated radiotherapy is used for newly diagnosed tumours, and stereotactic radiotherapy or radiosurgery for recurrence. Proton or heavy ion treatment might be considered near vulnerable brain structures or with favourable prognosis to avoid late toxicity, but RCTs must establish comparative tolerability, safety and efficacy. Conformal treatment requires reproducible immobilization and imaging-based positioning. Interstitial brachytherapy has not established a routine role. MRI at 3–4 weeks after radiotherapy supplies a new monitoring baseline.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy.
document_sections.content: Most drug treatments require physiological-range haematological, liver and kidney results and exclusion of major pulmonary or cardiac disease or infection before and during treatment. Most patients receive an alkylating agent during their disease course. Temozolomide is the most commonly used glioma drug; it is an oral DNA alkylator that crosses the blood–brain barrier. Its main dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, particularly thrombocytopenia, and liver function needs regular monitoring. Nitrosoureas such as lomustine, carmustine, nimustine and fotemustine cause later leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, at 4–6 weeks rather than 2–3 weeks, often with cumulative effects that may require interruption, dose reduction, discontinuation or another treatment. Pulmonary fibrosis is reported mainly with carmustine and rarely with lomustine. PCV combines lomustine, procarbazine and vincristine. Implanted carmustine wafers produced a modest OS benefit in newly diagnosed WHO grade 3 or 4 glioma or recurrent glioblastoma, but the pivotal trial found no statistically significant outcome difference after excluding WHO grade 3 cases from survival analysis. Benefits demonstrated for alkylating therapy in RCTs need weighing against late toxicity and a treatment-induced hypermutator phenotype linked to greater malignancy, particularly in longer-surviving patients with IDH-mutant disease. Bevacizumab, an anti-VEGF antibody, is approved for recurrent glioblastoma in the USA, Canada, Switzerland and other countries outside the European Union, without demonstrated OS benefit. Patients on systemic therapy should carry treatment records with laboratory results, complications and contraindications. Treating centres should maintain standardized procedures for chemotherapy delivery and complication management.

document_sections.heading: Monitoring and follow-up assessments.
document_sections.content: Observation without tissue verification risks understaging based on imaging alone and initially requires scans only 2–3 months apart. MRI alongside examination is the standard for disease-status and response assessment, using RANO criteria and consistent protocols. Following therapy, scans are commonly spaced 2–6 months apart according to histology; durable control and less aggressive tumours can justify longer intervals. Interpretation should consider the complete course of disease, particularly for untreated, slowly growing lesions. Suspected progression may warrant repeat MRI within 4–8 weeks. Pseudoprogression after chemoradiotherapy or immunotherapy and pseudoresponse after anti-angiogenic therapy occur most often during the first 3 months of treatment but can arise later. When uncertain, repeat imaging after 4–8 weeks is a pragmatic approach. Perfusion MRI and amino acid PET might help distinguish pseudoprogression from true progression. Biopsy is not invariably decisive: viable tumour cells can coexist with pseudoprogression. Patients should be offered counselling from specialist psychologists or nurses and palliative-care specialists; needs for occupational, speech and physical therapy and social-support counselling should be assessed.

document_sections.heading: Therapy — specific recommendations
document_sections.content: Treatment is differentiated by integrated glioma subtype, WHO grade, clinical condition, molecular markers, treatment history and whether disease is newly diagnosed or recurrent.

document_sections.heading: IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, WHO grade 2.
document_sections.content: Surgery is the primary treatment. Observation after surgery is justified following gross-total resection and potentially for patients aged <40 years after incomplete resection when symptomatic epilepsy is the only neurological manifestation. If further treatment is needed, radiotherapy followed by PCV is standard. Chemotherapy alone remains investigational but might reduce late cognitive risk for patients with large tumours and relatively favourable expected outcomes. Treatment at recurrence depends on initial management.

document_sections.heading: IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, WHO grade 3.
document_sections.content: Resection extent is prognostic. Separating WHO grades 2 and 3 remains controversial. Following gross-total removal, observation can also be considered for patients aged <40 years with grade 3 disease, no neurological deficits and, particularly, no homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion. In two large RCTs, adding PCV before or after first-line radiotherapy approximately doubled OS. Although the relevant molecularly defined cohorts were small, agreement between trials supports this standard of care. Unresolved questions concern long-term cognition and QOL after radiotherapy plus PCV and whether temozolomide-based chemoradiotherapy provides comparable OS. Long-term NOA-04 results found PCV or temozolomide alone was not superior to radiotherapy alone in any anaplastic-glioma molecular subgroup; chemotherapy alone is therefore unlikely to match radiotherapy followed by PCV. The modified CODEL trial will compare relevant strategies. At progression, treatment depends on prior treatment and response; another operation should always be considered. If first-line ineffectiveness or intolerance rules out both radiation and alkylating agents, bevacizumab may control symptoms, although its antitumour activity here is unknown and evidence does not support combining it with cytotoxic therapy.

document_sections.heading: IDH-mutant astrocytoma, WHO grade 2.
document_sections.content: Most WHO grade 2 astrocytomas have IDH mutations; gemistocytic astrocytoma is a distinct IDH-mutant grade 2 variant. Maximal safe resection is the preferred initial approach. Observation without an integrated diagnosis should be exceptional even for incidental lesions. Following gross-total resection, asymptomatic patients or those with seizures alone who are younger than the pragmatic ~40–45 years cut-off can be observed. Incomplete resection and/or age >40 years support consideration of involved-field radiotherapy at 50 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions. Early, rather than progression-delayed, radiotherapy prolonged PFS but not OS in a cited trial. Frontline chemotherapy alone remains investigational but might be used when radiotherapy is infeasible, for example with large tumours; temozolomide probably yields shorter PFS than radiotherapy in IDH-mutant grade 2 diffuse astrocytoma. RTOG 9802 reported OS increasing from 7.8 years to 13.3 years when PCV was added to 54 Gy radiotherapy for high-risk WHO grade 2 glioma: patients aged 18–39 years after subtotal resection or biopsy, or patients aged ≥40 years. Benefit appeared across histological subgroups and, in small molecular cohorts, for IDH-mutant astrocytomas or oligodendrogliomas but not IDH-wild-type tumours. Radiotherapy followed by PCV is therefore standard when postoperative treatment is indicated. At progression, neurological status, progression pattern and prior therapy guide treatment. Repeat surgery should always be considered, generally followed by radiotherapy if not previously given or by alkylating chemotherapy. Temozolomide is often favoured over PCV because of tolerability and easier administration.

document_sections.heading: Table 2 | Key treatment recommendations for adult patients with common diffuse gliomas
document_sections.content: The table compares treatment at diagnosis and at progression or recurrence across common integrated and NOS glioma categories. It includes initial observation where appropriate; radiotherapy followed by PCV or temozolomide; temozolomide chemoradiotherapy; and recurrence options including repeat surgery, nitrosoureas, temozolomide rechallenge, bevacizumab where available and, for previously unirradiated patients, radiotherapy. The accompanying notes recommend maximum safe resection whenever feasible, caution that benefit from another operation may depend on achieving gross-total removal, describe reirradiation indications as controversial and identify limited activity from renewed temozolomide or nitrosourea exposure without MGMT promoter methylation. Recommendations for NOS entities are based on low evidence; IDH-wild-type diffuse astrocytoma requires further molecular subclassification. Tumour-treating fields during maintenance temozolomide remain controversial despite a positive phase III trial and are not widely available in Europe.

document_sections.heading: IDH-mutant astrocytoma, WHO grade 3.
document_sections.content: The established approach begins with maximal resection or biopsy followed by radiotherapy at 60 Gy in 1.8–2 Gy fractions; its original evidence largely pooled WHO grade 3 subgroups with glioblastoma. NOA-04 found comparable PFS and OS with PCV or temozolomide alone versus radiotherapy alone. EORTC 26053 (CATNON) reported significantly longer OS with radiotherapy followed by 12 cycles of maintenance temozolomide, supporting this as standard care. The contribution of concurrent temozolomide remains uncertain: updated CATNON findings suggest limited additional improvement over maintenance and indicate chemotherapy benefit only for IDH-mutant tumours. At recurrence, prior therapy guides selection and another operation should be considered for everyone. After radiotherapy, reirradiation is an option following a minimum interval of ~12 months, but tumour size and recurrence pattern restrict use and efficacy remains uncertain without RCT data. Alkylating chemotherapy should be considered when disease progresses after radiotherapy and chemotherapy has not previously been given; temozolomide and nitrosoureas are probably similarly effective. In recurrent contrast-enhancing IDH-mutant glioma without 1p/19q codeletion, adding bevacizumab to temozolomide prolongs neither PFS nor OS.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations.
document_sections.content: IDH-mutant astrocytoma, WHO grade 2 needing further treatment should receive feasible resection or biopsy, involved-field radiotherapy and maintenance PCV (RTOG 9802) (C: II; L: B). For IDH-mutant astrocytoma, WHO grade 3, the standard comprises feasible resection or biopsy, involved-field radiotherapy and maintenance temozolomide (CATNON) (C: II; L: B). IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, WHO grade 2 requiring further treatment should receive radiotherapy followed by PCV (C: III; L: B); for WHO grade 3, radiotherapy followed by PCV is recommended on the basis of EORTC 26951 and RTOG 9402 (C: II; L: B). At progression after surgery and radiotherapy, temozolomide is standard for most patients with WHO grade 2 or 3 IDH-mutant glioma (C: II; L: B).

document_sections.heading: IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: This entity includes giant cell glioblastoma, gliosarcoma and epithelioid glioblastoma. Tumours formerly called IDH-mutant glioblastoma are now IDH-mutant astrocytoma, WHO grade 4 and may be managed along either IDH-wild-type glioblastoma or IDH-mutant grade 3 astrocytoma lines. Gross-total resection should be pursued where feasible. A small RCT in patients aged >65 years with WHO grade 3 or 4 glioma reported longer OS after resection than biopsy, but small sample size and between-group KPS imbalance make its relevance debatable. Standard glioblastoma radiotherapy at 60 Gy in 1.8–2 Gy fractions approximately doubled median OS in earlier evidence. In patients aged ≥70 years with KPS ≥70, 50 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions improved OS over best supportive care. With adverse age and/or KPS, hypofractionated 40 Gy in 15 fractions has activity similar to 60 Gy in 30 fractions. Further shortening to 5 × 5 Gy does not appear to reduce OS but could cause cognitive harm if improved systemic therapies lengthen older patients' survival. Accelerated regimens, brachytherapy, radiosurgery and stereotactic boosts have not improved OS over standard radiation. For newly diagnosed adults aged <70 years with good general and neurological condition, standard therapy is radiotherapy with daily temozolomide 75 mg/m2 throughout radiation, weekends included, followed by six maintenance cycles at 150–200 mg/m2 on 5 out of 28 days.

document_sections.heading: IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: Adding temozolomide to hypofractionated radiotherapy improved OS in patients aged ≥60 years; benefit is largely confined to MGMT promoter-methylated disease. NOA-08 and Nordic trial results support MGMT testing in older patients unsuitable for combination therapy: absent or unknown methylation favours hypofractionated radiotherapy alone, while methylated tumours should receive temozolomide alone on 5 out of 28 days until progression or for 12 months. Until 2016, the broad interpretation of trials was that omitting temozolomide caused no detriment in unmethylated disease. That interpretation became controversial after a small OS gain with radiotherapy plus temozolomide in older patients with unmethylated tumours and the negative CheckMate 498 result. An open-label phase III study reported better PFS and OS across subgroups when tumour-treating fields were added to maintenance temozolomide, without relevant between-arm QOL differences; nevertheless, its mechanism, absence of a sham control, data interpretation, wider-population QOL impact, feasibility and cost-effectiveness remain disputed. Supportive and palliative care is appropriate for patients with large or multifocal lesions and low KPS, especially when they cannot consent to further treatment after biopsy.

document_sections.heading: IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: Increasing temozolomide dose or continuing chemotherapy beyond six cycles has produced no reported benefit in newly diagnosed disease. Combining temozolomide and lomustine might extend OS in MGMT promoter-methylated glioblastoma, but its phase III trial was small, did not improve PFS and could consume lomustine before recurrence; use is largely confined to some German-speaking centres. Two phase III trials found that adding bevacizumab to temozolomide chemoradiotherapy extended PFS by 3–4 months without extending OS; a small phase II trial in older patients with unmethylated tumours produced similar findings. The clinical meaning of the PFS difference is uncertain because imaging-based progression assessment can be unreliable, and RTOG 0825 raised concern about early cognitive decline with bevacizumab. Bevacizumab is therefore generally not approved for newly diagnosed glioblastoma, though it could help highly symptomatic patients with large tumours tolerate radiotherapy. Phase III OS results were negative for rindopepimut in EGFRvIII-positive disease and for nivolumab in MGMT promoter-unmethylated disease.

document_sections.heading: IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: At recurrence, standards are poorly defined; prior treatment, age, KPS, MGMT status and progression pattern guide selection. Another operation is an option for ~20–30% of patients, commonly when a symptomatic, circumscribed relapse is diagnosed no earlier than 6 months after initial surgery. Earlier reoperation risks acting on pseudoprogression and is unlikely to provide lasting benefit if surgery and radiotherapy controlled disease for only a few months, although symptomatic early progression after inadequate initial surgery may justify it. Gross-total removal of enhancing recurrent tumour might improve survival after recurrence. Reirradiation efficacy and amino acid PET-assisted targeting remain debated. Larger lesions require smaller radiation fractions; approaches assessed include 5–6 Gy fractions to 30–36 Gy and single-dose radiosurgery at 15–20 Gy, with acceptable toxicity. The only RCT comparing bevacizumab plus radiotherapy against bevacizumab alone improved PFS but not OS.

document_sections.heading: IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: Systemic options at progression include nitrosoureas, repeat temozolomide, bevacizumab where available and clinical trials. Although lomustine 90–110 mg/m2 has not shown RCT superiority to another agent, its activity in control arms has led to increasing acceptance as a reference treatment; its 6-month PFS rate is ~20%. Alternative temozolomide schedules have yielded similar results, probably mainly in MGMT promoter-methylated tumours. RCTs do not establish that intensified temozolomide dosing outperforms standard dosing after a temozolomide-free interval. Bevacizumab lacks European Union approval for recurrence but received approval elsewhere on objective response rates of ~30% in two uncontrolled phase II trials. It has not been compared against placebo; adding it to lomustine did not improve OS over lomustine alone, and no bevacizumab combination partner has been identified that extends OS. Its principal routine role is temporary symptom relief and steroid sparing in symptomatic patients with large tumours. In other studies, nivolumab was not superior to bevacizumab and tumour-treating fields were not superior to physician-selected treatment. Targeted treatment has shown only a limited role. Approximately 50% of rare epithelioid glioblastomas carry BRAFV600E; this entity remains controversial because of resemblance to anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma. Patients with such tumours might benefit from BRAF inhibitors at recurrence.

document_sections.heading: Fig. 2 | Clinical pathway for IDH-mutant gliomas.
document_sections.content: The pathway begins with biopsy or resection and early postoperative MRI or CT (<48 h). For IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma and astrocytoma, grade, age, neurological deficits and tumour burden or residual tumour distinguish observation candidates from those directed toward radiotherapy followed by PCV or temozolomide; grade 4 astrocytoma follows a radiotherapy and temozolomide pathway. It shows neurological examination and imaging at 3–6-monthly intervals and identifies repeat surgery, alkylating chemotherapy, reirradiation, experimental treatment or palliative care as context-dependent options after progression.

document_sections.heading: Fig. 3 | Clinical pathway for IDH-wild-type glioblastomas, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: After biopsy or resection, the pathway calls for postoperative MRI or CT within <48h. Initial options depend on age, KPS and MGMT promoter methylation: temozolomide chemoradiotherapy, hypofractionated radiotherapy, temozolomide alone or palliative care according to the stated prognostic groups. Neurological examination and imaging are shown at 2–3-monthly intervals. At recurrence, KPS, neurological function and prior treatment inform consideration of another operation, alkylating chemotherapy, bevacizumab, reirradiation, experimental therapy or palliative care.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations.
document_sections.content: For IDH-wild-type glioblastoma in patients aged <70 years with KPS >70, standard care comprises feasible resection or biopsy, involved-field radiotherapy with concomitant temozolomide and six cycles of maintenance temozolomide (EORTC 26981-NCIC CE.3) (C: I; L: A). Temozolomide might have activity only in MGMT promoter-methylated tumours; activity in unmethylated disease is probably marginal (C: II; L: B). Older patients unsuitable for temozolomide chemoradiotherapy should be treated according to MGMT promoter methylation status, using radiotherapy such as 15 × 2.66 Gy or temozolomide alone on 5 out of 28 days (NOA-08, Nordic Trial) (C: II; L: B). At recurrence, standards are less certain. Surgery or radiotherapy might be considered; nitrosoureas, repeat temozolomide and bevacizumab subject to country-specific authorization are drug options, although OS benefit remains unproven. Appropriate trial enrolment should be considered when available (C: II; L: B).

document_sections.heading: H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: This entity accounts for the majority of diffuse brainstem, thalamic and spinal gliomas in children and adults. Surgery is limited. Benefit beyond radiotherapy is unestablished because the disease is rare and lacks dedicated trials. MGMT promoter methylation is usually absent, and prognosis is poor.

document_sections.heading: H3.3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma, WHO grade 4.
document_sections.content: These tumours arise predominantly in adolescents and young adults. MGMT promoter methylation is more common than its absence. Because they were previously classified as IDH-wild-type glioblastoma, chemoradiotherapy is considered a reasonable approach.

document_sections.heading: Discouraged treatments.
document_sections.content: Steroids should not treat oedema that is asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic and should be tapered as soon as possible because of their unfavourable long-term safety profile. In three separate large glioblastoma cohorts, steroid use was a negative prognostic factor for OS; it might also impede radiotherapy, chemotherapy or immunotherapy efficacy. Continuing any treatment, including bevacizumab or tumour-treating fields, after confirmed progression on that treatment is discouraged because clinical benefit has not been established. Irinotecan and platinum compounds are known not to be active against gliomas and should not be used for them. Use outside a clinical trial of inadequately tested concepts is discouraged, including CUSP9, cannabinoids, methadone, sulfasalazine and valproate; the exception for valproate is seizure control.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: WHO classification changes have substantially altered routine glioma diagnosis and management. Multidisciplinary tumour boards should guide care throughout the disease course, including choices between local and specialist-centre treatment, inpatient and outpatient care, and appropriate neurorehabilitation. Local, national and EANO guidance offer additional direction. Guidance reflects evidence and consensus at a particular time. Specific treatment and outcome data remain unavailable for many newly defined entities, making extrapolation from earlier trials difficult. Well-designed, molecularly enriched RCTs are needed to substantiate some recommendations.
